title: How Ryup scores your morning: inside the scoring engine
excerpt: How Ryup turns your spoken answers into one fair 0 to 100 score: five measured signals, an AI judge, anti-cheating caps, newcomer warm-up and safe retries.
content:
Every morning, Ryup asks you to do something small and hard at the same time. You read a short passage aloud, answer a few questions, and finish with a short affirmation about your own day. Then the app shows you one number from 0 to 100.

That number looks simple. Behind it sits a scoring engine that has to be fair, hard to cheat, explainable, and safe to run at 6 AM when thousands of people finish at nearly the same moment.

This post explains how that engine works, in plain words. It follows one morning from the moment you stop recording to the moment the score appears. Along the way it explains the design choices, including the ones we got wrong at first.

## Words you will see in this post

- **Transcript**: your spoken words, written down by a speech-to-text service.
- **Word error rate (WER)**: the share of words you read differently from the original text. A WER of 0.10 means about one word in ten was different.
- **LLM judge**: a large language model, the same kind of AI behind chat assistants, that reads the content and your answers and grades them against a fixed rubric.
- **Gate**: a rule that puts a ceiling on the score when something specific happened, such as skipping the affirmation.
- **Queue**: a waiting line of work. Here, each finished morning waits in line to be scored.
- **Idempotent**: safe to run twice. Doing it a second time gives the same result and breaks nothing.

## The big picture

When you finish your morning, the phone uploads your recordings to storage and tells our backend that the session is complete. The backend does not make you wait on that request. It marks the session as "pending score" and puts it in a queue. A background worker picks it up, scores it, and then sends you a notification that your score is ready.

Here is the whole path:

![How a spoken morning becomes one score](/blog/ryup/06-scoring-pipeline.svg)

The scoring rules live in one small Go package that does pure math. It has no network calls, no database and no clock. Everything it needs is handed to it as plain data, and it returns a result. Another package, the pipeline, does the messy work: downloading audio, calling vendors, saving results. Keeping the two apart is the most useful decision in the whole design, and we will come back to why.

## Step 1: turning your voice into words

Each recording is sent to a speech-to-text service (we use ElevenLabs). It returns the words, when each word started and ended, and how confident it was about each one.

Two details matter here.

**Transcription happens in parallel, but with a limit.** A morning can have a handful of recordings, and several people finish at once. So the pipeline transcribes recordings side by side, but passes every call through one process-wide gate. The limit belongs to our account with the vendor, not to any one morning, so the gate protects the vendor from the sum of all mornings. If the vendor says "slow down", we stop the calls still running instead of making the rush worse.

**The order is fixed.** Results come back in whatever order they finish, so the pipeline puts them back in the order you spoke them. This sounds like a small thing. It matters because the text is later turned into a fingerprint, and the same morning must always produce the same fingerprint. If the order floated around, a retry would score differently from the first attempt.

Every transcript is saved the moment it arrives. We paid for it, so a later failure must never make us pay twice.

## Step 2: five measured signals

The engine does not ask one big question. It measures five separate things, each one scored from 0 to 100, and each one carrying a **confidence** between 0 and 1. Confidence is how much we trust that measurement this time. A shaky transcription gets lower confidence, and a lower confidence means that component counts for less.

Here are the five, with the weight each one carries in the final mix.

| Signal | Weight | What it asks |
|---|---|---|
| Response quality | 28 | Did you understand the content and answer the questions? |
| Word accuracy | 22 | Did you read the passage faithfully? |
| Affirmation | 20 | Did you finish with a real, personal affirmation? |
| Audio liveliness | 15 | Did you sound awake? |
| Interaction quality | 15 | Did you take part fully and for a real length of time? |

The weights add up to 100 by convention. The top weight goes to response quality because engaging with the content is the closest thing to "my brain is actually on", which is the promise of the product.

### Word accuracy: reading what is on the page

We compare the passage you were shown with your transcript, word by word, and compute the word error rate. A WER of 0.05 or less scores 100. A WER of 0.60 or more scores 0. Between those two points the score falls in a straight line, so a WER of 0.20 scores about 73.

One feature here deserves a mention. Many Ryup users speak Hindi, English or a mix of both, often called Hinglish. Speech-to-text tools spell Hinglish words in more than one valid way. So the comparison is forgiving in a careful way. Two words count as the same if they differ by one letter and both are at least four letters long, or by two letters and both are at least eight letters long. Short words must match exactly. This stops us from marking someone wrong for a spelling choice the transcription tool made.

When the passage is very short, fewer than five words, we cap the confidence of this component at 0.5. A tiny sample is weak evidence, and the math says so.

### Response quality: the AI judge

Reading aloud can be done half asleep. Understanding what you read cannot, at least not as easily. So one component asks an AI model to grade how you engaged.

The judge receives the content you were served, the questions asked, and your answers, in order. It returns four scores from 0 to 5: relevance, understanding, substance and effort. It also returns a short mood note and a celebratory one-line reason for the app to show. The rubric has rules we wrote down in plain language, and two of them are worth repeating:

- **Understanding is judged only against the source text we supplied.** The judge may not use its own knowledge of the world. If the story says the hero was named Asha, the answer is graded against that story.
- **Hindi and Hinglish are first-class.** The judge grades meaning, never accent or English polish.

The model's reply must be strict JSON, a machine-readable format. We validate it, clamp every value into the 0 to 5 range, and require the four core fields. If the reply is malformed we ask once more.

The component score is simple: add the four numbers, divide by 20, multiply by 100. Scores of 4, 3, 3 and 4 give 14 out of 20, which is 70.

A rule we learned the hard way sits right here, and we will tell that story below.

### Audio liveliness: pace and pauses

This component asks whether you sounded awake. It uses two things we can measure from the word timings in the transcript, with no audio analysis at all:

- **Pace**: words per minute. The ideal band is 90 to 160. The score falls to 0 at 40 or at 260.
- **Pause ratio**: the share of the time you were silent. Up to 35 percent silence is ideal, falling to 0 at 70 percent.

The two are mixed with weights of 0.4 and 0.3. The engine also has a slot for voice energy, but for recorded sessions we do not measure it, so the weights re-balance over the two that exist. A person speaking at 120 words per minute with 50 percent silence scores 100 on pace and about 57 on pauses, so the component is about 82.

That re-balancing idea shows up everywhere in this engine, and it has a name in our design notes: **missing is not zero**. If we could not measure something, we leave it out and divide the weight among what we did measure. We never punish you for a gap on our side.

### Interaction quality: taking part

This looks at how fully you took part: how many of the questions you answered, and how long the whole session lasted. A real session length is between about 2 and 3.5 minutes. Very short sessions score low, and so do extremely long ones. Answer every question and you score 100 on that part.

Response time per question is also part of the design, but the app does not send turn timings today, so it is absent, and the component carries slightly lower confidence (0.8) because of that. Again, absent, not zero.

### Affirmation: the closing line

Each session ends with a short self-directed affirmation, such as "I will finish my work today and call my mother". The affirmation component mixes three things: its length (12 to 25 seconds is ideal), whether the AI judge found it to be a genuine first-person affirmation, and how it was delivered. The last piece, delivery, is based on pace because energy is not measured.

If the affirmation is missing entirely, the component is skipped and a gate caps the score. That brings us to the next step.

## Step 3: combining the five into one number

The combining step is a weighted average, but with one twist: each component counts for its weight multiplied by its confidence, and only components that were actually measured take part.

```
effective = weight x confidence
raw score = sum(effective x score) / sum(effective)
```

A worked example makes it concrete. Suppose a typical good morning gives these scores, all at full confidence: word accuracy 82, response quality 75, liveliness 68, interaction 90, affirmation 85.

```
(22 x 82 + 28 x 75 + 15 x 68 + 15 x 90 + 20 x 85) / 100
= (1804 + 2100 + 1020 + 1350 + 1700) / 100
= 79.74, shown as 80
```

Now imagine there was no passage to read that morning, so word accuracy is absent. The weights of the remaining four are re-balanced over their own total, so you are not penalised for the activity mix.

## Step 4: the order of the rules

After the average comes a short list of rules. The order matters, and it was chosen deliberately.

![The order in which the rules change the score](/blog/ryup/06-score-formula.svg)

**1. Honest-behaviour gates (they cap, never subtract).**
- No affirmation: the score cannot be above 70.
- Less than 20 seconds of your speech in total: the score cannot be above 40. A two or three minute activity with under 20 seconds of voice was not really done, whatever the math says.

Skipping the affirmation shows why gates exist. Say you aced everything else with a raw 91. The cap brings it to 70, and the app can say, "Great session. Finish with your affirmation tomorrow to unlock your full score." That single line is the whole behavioural nudge.

**2. The alarm retry penalty.** Waking on the first ring is part of waking up well, so each extra time the alarm had to ring before you finished costs 5 points, counting at most three retries. The worst case is minus 15. This is the only place the engine subtracts points, because retrying is not suspicious, it is simply weaker wake-up behaviour. It is applied after the gates so it can never hide under a cap that was going to bind anyway, and the app can show exactly why: "minus 10 because the alarm rang twice more."

**3. The newcomer warm-up curve.** A brand-new user who has a rough first week should not be crushed by it. So new people see a softened score, and the softening fades over their first 15 scored sessions. At zero sessions the shown score is `100 - (100 - raw) x 0.65`, so a raw 45 appears as 64. By session 15 the factor reaches 1 and what you see is exactly what was measured.

**4. The abuse caps, applied after everything else.**
- **Replay suspected**: cap 25. If the words you said this morning are a near duplicate of a morning in the past 14 days, we suspect a recording or a script. We compute a fingerprint of the speech and compare it. The cap is 25, not 0, because collisions and genuine coincidence exist, so we leave a floor.
- **Flagged content**: cap 10. A moderation check, its own small AI call, flags abusive or hateful speech. Again, a floor and not zero, because false positives exist, and the session is put in front of a human.

The abuse caps come after the newcomer curve on purpose. Leniency can soften an honest rough morning. It must never cushion cheating or abuse.

One more rule on moderation: if the check itself fails, the session is scored as clean and the check is retried next time. We never punish anyone on a guess.

### Two scores, on purpose

The engine produces two numbers every time: the **shown** score (softened for newcomers) and a **strict** score (unsoftened). The app shows you the first. Anything that compares people, such as the rating system, only ever uses the strict one. The design phrase is "show lenient, compete strict". It means a new account can never gain an unfair rank from the warm-up curve.

### One tip, chosen by rules

The result also carries a tip code for "the one thing to improve tomorrow". It is picked by plain rules, in priority order: flagged content, replay, no affirmation, too little speech, heavy alarm retrying, and then the weakest component. If every component scored 90 or more, the tip is "keep it up" instead of nitpicking. The backend only picks a code, and the app turns it into friendly localised copy. The same idea applies to the score band (for example "strong" or "building"), so the reason line can never contradict the number.

## From a good morning to a morning score

The 0 to 100 engagement score describes how well you did the activity. A separate number, the **morning score**, describes how consistently you wake up early. They are related, but they are not the same thing.

A session counts as a qualifying morning only if all of these hold:

- the app sent a real time zone for that day;
- the ring you woke up to matches an alarm saved on the server;
- that ring happened between 04:00 and 08:00 local time, inclusive;
- you finished the activity within 15 minutes of that ring.

If a morning does not qualify, the app is told exactly why, and never silently. When it does qualify, the tier is decided by the ring you actually woke to, not the time the alarm was set for:

| Ring time | Tier | Bonus points |
|---|---|---|
| 04:00 to 04:59 | A | 15 |
| 05:00 to 05:59 | B | 10 |
| 06:00 to 06:59 | C | 5 |
| 07:00 to 08:00 | D | 0 |

Morning points are `0.85 x score + bonus`. A score of 80 at a 6:30 ring gives 68 plus 5, which is 73. Your morning score moves toward today's points as a running average, so one great morning does not leap it upward and one bad one does not wreck it.

![Morning tiers, decay ladder and the strict rating lane](/blog/ryup/06-morning-and-rating.svg)

Missed days are handled with care. A **freeze credit** from a shared pool protects a missed day completely, and the score does not move. With no credits left, the miss climbs a gentle ladder: the score shrinks by 1 percent, then 2, then 5, then 10 percent for each further missed day. Each qualifying morning steps you one rung back down the ladder. Two safety rules sit on top. The score can never fall below 40 percent of your all-time best, and a missed day can never raise a score.

## Running it safely at 6 AM

Scoring is cheap per morning but spiky in time. Everyone who wakes at 6:30 finishes within the same few minutes. So the pipeline is built around one question: what happens when something goes wrong in the middle?

![What can go wrong, and what the pipeline does about it](/blog/ryup/06-failure-handling.svg)

**The queue is the database column, not memory.** A session's scoring status lives in the database. A scan every 30 seconds reads the queue. If a request to wake the worker is lost, the next scan finds the session anyway. Before this design, a phone that was pocketed meant a morning might never be retried until the next deploy.

**Eight workers, one process-wide vendor gate.** Eight mornings can be scored at once. The vendor gate, not the number of workers, controls how hard we lean on the speech vendor.

**Each attempt has a time budget.** One attempt gets ten minutes. A lease marks that a worker owns a session, and it lasts twenty minutes, which is deliberately longer than the budget. A test asserts that relationship, because shortening the lease would cause a slow-but-alive attempt to be retried alongside itself.

**Five attempts with growing waits.** The waits are 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 8 minutes and 30 minutes, with random jitter added. Only ever adding jitter, never subtracting, is deliberate: every session that fails in one vendor outage fails at the same instant, and without jitter they would all retry in the same second and knock the recovering vendor over again.

**Not every failure is the same failure.** A rate limit means we asked too often, which is our capacity problem, not the user's. So the session is held without spending an attempt. A rejected API key is an operator problem, so it is held too, and scores once the key is fixed. A permanent error, such as an unreadable audio file, gives up at once because a retry cannot help. Holds are bounded to twelve hours so nothing waits forever.

**A panic in one session stays in that session.** Go can crash a whole program on an unexpected error. Every worker and every transcription goroutine has its own recovery, so one bad morning never takes the server down.

**Our failure never costs you.** This is the standing rule of the whole system. If we give up on a morning, because the retry budget is spent or a bug stopped it, you are compensated with a day, and the reason is recorded. A lost morning is never silently a missed one.

**A spending backstop.** Each morning has a cost ceiling of about two dollars and a ceiling of 200 paid calls. Those numbers were not guessed. They come from our own limits: at most 5 attempts, 4 model calls per attempt, 1,024 output tokens each, which works out to a worst case of around 70 cents. Our own estimate for a normal morning is about one cent. The ceiling is roughly three times the worst case that obeys every limit, so reaching it means a limit failed, a bug rather than a busy morning. Crossing it stops the morning and compensates the person, and it is recorded as its own reason so a runaway loop is not mistaken for an ordinary vendor outage.

## Explainable, replayable and private

Every score row stores the configuration version that produced it, a numbers-only snapshot of the inputs, the gates that applied, the penalty, the tip and the band.

The snapshot holds no transcript text and no audio, only numbers. That keeps an important promise: the score table survives account deletion untouched because it holds nothing personal. It also gives us a powerful tool. Because the scoring package is pure, we can take any stored snapshot and **replay** it under a candidate configuration, and see exactly how real past mornings would have scored. Tuning becomes a safe offline experiment instead of a guess.

Versioning matters because tuning any number means a new version. Our current version is v5. It exists because of a bug in our thinking, not in the code. Earlier, if the AI judge answered only on its second attempt, we counted its grade at lower confidence. Two people who said the same words got different scores, and the only difference was whether our vendor answered us first time. They were never told, and nothing they did could change it. Worse, lowering one component's confidence did not simply lower the score. It moved the other weights around, so it changed the number in an unpredictable direction. We removed it. A retried judgment now scores exactly like a first-try one. We still record how often our vendor needs a second ask, because that is worth knowing, but it no longer touches anybody's number.

Deleted accounts are handled before any money is spent. A session whose owner has deleted their account is withdrawn from the queue, and nothing is scored or compensated.

## What we would tell another team

- **Keep the rules pure.** Scoring math with no network and no clock can be tested to the decimal, replayed forever and changed without fear.
- **Treat missing data as missing.** Re-balance the weights over what was measured. Never let a vendor gap look like a bad result.
- **Order your rules on purpose.** Whether a penalty comes before or after a cap, or before or after a softening curve, changes who it hurts. Write the order down.
- **Separate what is shown from what is compared.** A kind score for the person and a strict score for fairness can both be true.
- **Give every failure its own treatment.** Rate limits, bad keys, bad audio and bugs deserve different responses.
- **Never let your failure cost the user.** Build the compensation path before you build the retry path.
- **Put a ceiling on spend.** Derive it from your own limits so that a number is a statement, not a guess.

The score is only half of the story. The other half is deciding what content you are served each morning in the first place. That is the recommendation engine, and we describe it in [how Ryup recommends your morning content](/blog/how-ryup-recommends-your-morning-content). The server that runs all of this is described in [the Go backend post](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)
author: Softogram
coverAlt: Diagram: voice recordings are transcribed, moderated and judged by an AI model, turned into five components, combined with weights, capped by gates, reduced by a retry penalty, softened for newcomers and saved as one score.

title: How Ryup recommends your morning content, without ML
excerpt: Inside Ryup's recommendation engine: taste scores that fade, a 10 slot morning plan, a four step discovery ladder, a seeded weighted shuffle and safe fallbacks.
content:
Every Ryup morning starts with a question that sounds easy: what should this person read and talk about today?

If we pick badly, the morning is boring, and a boring morning is the first thing a person skips. If we only repeat what someone already likes, the app goes stale. If we pick at random, we waste their time. A recommendation engine is the part of the backend that tries to get this right, every day, for every person.

This post explains how ours works. It does not use machine learning, and that is a choice we will defend. It is a transparent set of rules and a small amount of arithmetic that anyone on the team can read, debug at 6 AM, and tune without a deploy.

## Words you will see in this post

- **Content type**: a broad kind of activity, such as a story, a news item, a joke or an affirmation.
- **Category**: a smaller topic inside a type, such as "horror" inside stories or "stock market" inside news.
- **Affinity**: a number that says how much a person likes something. Higher means more liked. Negative means disliked.
- **Event**: one recorded reaction, such as a thumbs up or a tap on "change this".
- **Half-life**: the time it takes for a value to fall to half. The same idea is used to describe radioactive material.
- **Weighted shuffle**: shuffling a list so that entries with a bigger weight are more likely to land near the top, but not guaranteed to.
- **Cold start**: the situation where we know nothing yet about a brand-new person.
- **Seed**: a starting number for a random generator. The same seed always produces the same "random" order.

## Why not machine learning?

It is the first question people ask, so here is the direct answer.

A typical learned recommender needs a lot of data from a lot of people before it beats simple rules. Ryup has a small number of content types, and each type has a few dozen categories. That is a candidate space of a few hundred things, not millions. Ranking a few hundred scored candidates needs arithmetic, not a model.

Simple rules also have three advantages we care about more than cleverness:

1. **You can explain any result.** When someone asks "why did I get a horror story today?", we can answer with a replayable list of events. A black box cannot do that.
2. **You can fix it at 6 AM.** If the engine misbehaves, a person can read the numbers and see why.
3. **It can be tuned without a deploy.** Every number lives in a database row, as we will see.

The design leaves room to grow. Everything that a learned system would need later, mainly a clean log of what people did, is saved from day one. We come back to that at the end.

## The loop in one picture

The engine only touches three moments in a person's life with the app, and nothing runs during the live activity itself.

![The recommendation loop](/blog/ryup/07-recommendation-loop.svg)

1. **Onboarding.** At signup you choose the content types you like. We never ask about categories. They are learned from behaviour. Each type you pick starts with a warm score instead of a neutral one.
2. **Each morning, before you start.** The backend builds your plan for the day from your stored scores, saves it, and hands the app the list.
3. **After the session.** Your reactions are saved as events, and your scores are updated.

The most important structural decision is the last one on the list: the live part of the product stays fast and simple, and all the thinking happens before or after it.

## How the engine is built

The engine is a pure Go package. Pure means it never touches the network, the database or the clock. It receives plain inputs and returns plain outputs. Even randomness is injected as a seeded generator. A thin layer around it reads from Postgres, calls the pure package, and writes results back.

That is the same pattern we used for the scoring engine. It makes every function easy to test and lets us replay history under a different setting, which matters later.

Six tables hold everything:

| Table | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `preference_events` | An append-only log of every reaction. The permanent ground truth. |
| `user_type_affinities` | One current score per person per content type. |
| `user_category_affinities` | One current score per person per category. |
| `session_offers` | The plan made each morning, and what happened to each slot. |
| `category_trend_scores` | A daily summary of what is popular across everyone. |
| `personalization_configs` | The versioned settings for the engine. |

A natural question is why we keep both an event log and score tables. The scores are a **cache** of the log. The morning plan runs at alarm time and must be one cheap indexed read, not an aggregation over a person's entire history. But the log is the truth. If a bug ever damages the score tables, we rebuild them by replaying the log, and the same replay lets us test a candidate configuration on real histories.

## What the engine learns from

Every reaction is a signal with a weight. The engine's configuration defines ten of them. These are the defaults:

| Signal | Weight | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Picked this type at signup | +5 | Onboarding |
| Told us they like something | +8 | They said so |
| Thumbs up | +10 | The app |
| Thumbs down | -10 | The app |
| "Change this one" (swap) | -6 on the category, -2 on the type | The app |
| Accepted an offer | +2 | Session outcome |
| Rejected an offer | -2 (but -1 if it was a recommendation) | Session outcome |
| Finished the activity | +1 | Session lifecycle |
| High engagement (strict score 80 or more) | +2 | Scoring engine |
| Low engagement (strict score 40 or less) | -1 | Scoring engine |

The ranking of those weights follows one principle: **explicit beats implicit**. A thumb is worth ten points, and a finished activity is worth one, because telling us what you want is always stronger than us guessing from behaviour.

**An honest note on what is live.** Today the app records four of these as taste events: the signup choice, the thumbs up and thumbs down, and the swap. The offer outcome is recorded too, and it feeds the repeat guard and the comeback timing, but it does not move a score yet. The engagement and "finished the activity" signals have weights in the configuration and a place in the design, but nothing writes them as events yet. We list them because the engine is built to accept them with a configuration change, not a rewrite. We would rather say that plainly than claim a feature the code does not have.

How a morning's offers get their outcome is a good example of a careful assumption. In a recorded morning there is no conversation to read, so a slot you recorded an answer for counts as accepted, and a slot you swapped counts as swapped. A skipped slot and an unreached one look identical from our side, so neither is ever counted as a rejection. We do not turn silence into a dislike.

A few details worth explaining:

- **A swap hurts the category more than the type.** If you tap "change this story", you are mostly saying "not this topic", not "I hate stories". So the category takes the full minus 6, and the type takes only minus 2.
- **Rejecting a recommendation is cheap.** When we try something new on you and you say no, it costs only 1 point instead of 2. Trying new things must never be punished, or the engine would stop exploring.
- **High and low engagement are defined to use the strict score.** The thresholds are written against the scoring engine's unsoftened number, so the newcomer warm-up can never inflate our idea of what a new person likes. This is where the two engines are designed to meet.
- **Some things are deliberately not signals.** Being shown an item is not evidence of liking it. How hard someone woke up is about sleep, not taste. And a flagged-content session says nothing about preference. Only reactions count.
- **"Unclear" writes nothing.** The written design for reading reactions out of a spoken conversation says an ambiguous reply produces no event at all. A missed signal costs almost nothing. A wrong signal pollutes the profile. The same attitude shows in the offer outcome rule above.

## Taste fades: the half-life rule

A preference is not permanent. Someone who loved horror stories in March may have moved on by May. So every score fades over time, and the fade follows the half-life idea.

```
effective = stored x 0.5 ^ (days since last event / 30)
```

With a half-life of 30 days, a score is worth half after 30 days of silence, a quarter after 60 days, and so on. When a new reaction arrives, we first decay the old value up to now, then add the new weight, then clamp the result to a range of minus 50 to plus 50. The clamp stops any favourite from building an unassailable lead and stops a dislike from digging a bottomless hole.

![How a thumbs up fades and when it stops being a favourite](/blog/ryup/07-taste-decay.svg)

Here is what that means for one person. They give a category a thumbs up, worth +10. Thirty days later it is worth 5. Sixty days later it is worth 2.5. The line for "favourite" sits at 3, so after about 52 days of silence that category quietly stops being one of their favourites, unless they react to it again. Recent reactions always beat old ones, without anyone having to delete anything.

The interpretation lines over the effective value are simple:

- **3 or more**: a favourite.
- **8 or more**: a strong like.
- **minus 3 or less**: a mild dislike.
- **minus 15 or less**: muted. Muted categories are left out of personal picks.

Because the faded value is calculated when we read it, nothing has to run overnight to age the scores. The stored number never changes by itself.

## Building the morning plan

Now the main event. The plan is a **list of lists**.

The outer list has 10 slots. Each slot is one pairing of a type and a category, such as "stories, comedy" or "news, stock market". Each slot carries an inner list of up to 10 concrete items. The plan always ends with one more slot, **free choice**, which is never shuffled and always succeeds.

![The ten slot plan and the discovery ladder](/blog/ryup/07-morning-plan.svg)

### The seven personal slots

Seven slots come from your favourites. For each content type, the engine takes the categories at or above the favourite line, best first, capped at 10 per type. All of them go into one pool, and the engine draws seven from that pool using the weighted draw described below, so a higher score means a higher chance of making the cut. Three guards keep this from going wrong:

- **No one type may take more than three slots**, so a single content type cannot fill the whole morning.
- **A repeat guard** removes categories you accepted in the last two mornings, so mornings do not copy each other. People with fewer than three favourites are exempt, so a small pool is never starved.
- **Muted categories and empty categories never get a slot.**

**Cold start** is handled by a fallback: with no favourites yet, the pool becomes the categories of the types you chose at signup. Selection rotates through them, least recently served first. A brand-new person still gets a sensible morning.

### The three recommendation slots

This is the exploration part. Three slots come from a four-step **ladder**. Slot one starts at step one of the ladder, slot two at step two, and slot three at step three. If a step has nothing to offer, the slot rolls down to the next step.

1. **Lapsed favourites.** "You loved this, but not lately." Categories where your stored score was a strong like (8 or more) but you have had no positive reaction for 14 days. The stronger the old love, the higher it ranks. If you reject one of these comeback offers, the engine waits 30 days before offering it again, then 60, then 120.
2. **Trending this week.** "People are enjoying this, and you have not tried it." A daily job adds up the positive reactions of everyone over the last 7 days, per category, and rewrites a small table. Your favourites and muted categories are excluded. If that table is more than 48 hours old, it is treated as stale and skipped.
3. **Similar to what you like.** A planned feature that will use meaning-based comparisons between categories, so a reader who loves stock market news may be offered crypto news. In the code today this step is an empty placeholder. Its rung stays in the ladder so that slots roll down past it correctly.
4. **Never-tried types.** Content types you did not pick and have never reacted to, ranked by how popular they are. This is how a brand-new content type reaches everyone.

If the whole ladder is empty, the slot falls back to your next personal pick. If that is empty too, the slot is dropped, and the plan is just shorter. It is never empty, because the free-choice slot is always there.

We also record why each slot exists. Every stored slot carries a source label: favourite, lapsed favourite, trending, similar, new type, type backfill or free choice. Later we can ask a plain SQL question, such as "which source do people accept most?", and learn which part of the engine is earning its place.

## The weighted shuffle: random, but fair

Once the ten slots are chosen, their order must be decided. We want the order to change from day to day, so that mornings feel alive, but we do not want it uniformly random. A favourite should usually lead.

The tool is a **weighted shuffle**. Each slot gets a weight, and the weight sets its chance of landing on top. A simple example with three entries weighing 60, 30 and 10: the first leads about 60 percent of mornings, the second 30 and the third 10. When the first does not lead, it most often sits second.

For personal slots, the weight is the effective score plus 20, with a floor of 1 so that every weight stays positive. Say your three favourite categories score 16, 8 and 4. Their weights are 36, 28 and 24, which gives them first-place chances of about 41, 32 and 27 percent. Even your weakest favourite leads more than a quarter of the time, which keeps the plan from becoming predictable.

Recommendation slots use the same formula, so they compete on honest terms. A lapsed favourite uses its stored score. The most popular trending category maps to the top of the score range. A never-tried type uses a default score of 5. A recommendation can lead your morning, but only as often as its score deserves.

### How the shuffle works

The implementation is a short, well-known trick (the Efraimidis-Spirakis method). Each entry draws a random number `u` between 0 and 1, and gets the key `u ^ (1 / weight)`. Sorting by key, largest first, gives exactly the same result as drawing one entry at a time in proportion to weight. It needs one pass and no loops, and it is easy to test.

### Seeded, so a retry does not flicker

The random generator is seeded with the person's ID and their local date. That gives us three properties at once:

- The same person on the same day gets an **identical plan** if the plan is built twice. The prefetch might run twice, and the screen must not change under someone's thumb.
- The next day gives a **fresh draw**.
- Different people draw **independently** of each other.

Nothing else in the entire engine uses randomness. Everything below the shuffle is deterministic and explainable. If a plan looks strange, we can reproduce it by fixing the seed.

## Choosing the items inside each slot

Each slot's inner list holds up to 10 items. Items do not have a per-person score, so they are ordered by novelty and freshness:

- **A never-seen item** weighs 100.
- **A seen item** weighs the number of days since it was last seen, capped at 30.
- **A new item**, curated in the last 7 days, gets a bonus of 20.

There is also a hard rule, set by the founder: **an item you have already seen can never outrank one you have not.** The engine splits items into unseen and seen before the draw, shuffles each group on its own, and fills the list from the unseen group first. It only reaches seen items once the unseen ones run out.

### The exception: affirmations come back

The rule above is wrong for one kind of content. When you love an affirmation, hearing it again is the point, the way a favourite song returns. So content types can have their own **novelty rule**. For affirmations, seen items compete in the same draw as unseen ones, and an item you liked weighs 1.5 times an unseen one (150 against 100). A liked affirmation comes back sometimes, not every morning, and new lines keep arriving. Every other type keeps the standard rule exactly as before.

### "Change this one"

Each slot's inner list is also the path for swaps. When you tap "change this", the backend:

1. Locks that slot's row, so two taps arriving together cannot both advance it.
2. Reads the replacement content **before** committing the move. The other order could leave you advanced past an item you never received, and it would be gone for good.
3. Records the swap as a signal: minus 6 on the category, minus 2 on the type.
4. Advances the slot and marks both items as seen.

Repeats are treated as normal. If a request comes from a double tap or a retry, and the item is not the one currently in front of you, the queue does not move, and the response just returns what you are looking at now. That endpoint runs at 6 AM on whatever signal the bedroom has, and advancing twice would cost content you never saw.

## When the engine breaks

A recommendation bug must never break an alarm. So the engine has three layers of defence.

**The configuration has a three-level fallback.** The engine reads its settings from the database and refreshes them every 60 seconds, validating every key and range. If the database row is missing or invalid, it keeps the last known good copy in memory. If there is no such copy, for instance the database was unreachable at startup, it uses defaults compiled into the program. Each step logs loudly. This is how we can tune a number without a deploy and still survive an empty config table.

**Settings are immutable versions.** Tuning a number means inserting a new version row and flipping one active flag. Nobody edits a live row. Every event and every stored plan is stamped with the version in force, so history never silently changes its meaning.

**Failure falls back to the old behaviour.** If anything in the engine fails, such as missing rows, bad settings or a panic, the app catches it and serves the pre-personalisation morning: all types shown, the person picks, and plain rotation chooses the content. This is a hard requirement, asserted by a dedicated test rather than only written in a document.

There is one more naming detail that came from a real bug. Slots added just to make sure every content type appears were once stored as "rotation", a label documented as meaning something entirely different, a plan where the whole engine had failed. One label for two situations made the acceptance numbers impossible to read. They now have their own label, `type_backfill`.

## How we know it is working

Everything is measurable with plain SQL, per configuration version. The core question is the acceptance rate by source and by position. If lapsed favourites are accepted far more often than trending picks, we learn that and can change the ladder. If the same slot is rejected morning after morning, the weights are wrong. Because each stored plan records the version and the reason for every slot, the answers are specific.

## What comes next

None of the following needs a schema change, which is the point of keeping an append-only log from the first day:

1. **Similarity between categories**, using embeddings (lists of numbers that place a topic by meaning) stored in Postgres with a free extension. They would be computed ahead of time into an ordinary table, so the morning plan never does vector math.
2. **Mood-aware serving.** The scoring engine already stores a short mood note each morning. After enough mornings, someone who is flat on Mondays might get comedy on Mondays.
3. **Learning from other people**, such as "people who like dark jokes also like horror stories", once there are enough active people to beat noise.
4. **Tuned weights**, learned from measured acceptance by source, while still keeping the serving step deterministic.

Each of these is earned by data volume, not built on day one.

## What we would tell another team

- **Start with rules and an event log.** Transparent arithmetic over an append-only log is a stronger foundation than a model you cannot explain. The log keeps every smarter option open.
- **Let old taste fade.** One half-life rule gives you recency for free, with no cleanup job.
- **Keep explicit signals stronger than implicit ones.** Believe what people tell you.
- **Make trying new things cheap.** Penalise a rejected recommendation less than a rejected favourite, or the engine will stop exploring.
- **Randomise the order, not the choice.** A seeded weighted shuffle keeps mornings fresh while staying explainable and repeatable.
- **Always end the list with a way out.** A free-choice slot means the engine can never trap anyone.
- **Never let a recommendation bug break the product.** Build the plain fallback first, and test it.
